newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan court orders KAL to pay victims' families.
newsitem.headline: Japan court orders KAL to pay victims' families.

text.p: A Japanese court on Wednesday ordered Korean Airlines (KAL) to pay damages to the families of four Japanese passengers killed in the September 1983 shoot-down of a KAL plane over the Soviet Union.

Judge Ko Ito of the Tokyo District Court ordered KAL to pay 136 million yen ($1.18 million) in damages to the families, saying the airline company was responsible for flying the Boeing 747 jet for five hours over Soviet territory.
"The defendant cannot escape bearing responsibility for the act of negligence. The crew failed to recognise that the aircraft was off its course for five hours," Judge Ito said.
It was the first ruling by a Japanese court on the liability of a carrier in an aircraft accident outside Japan.
KAL flight 007, bound for Seoul from New York, was shot down by a Soviet fighter on September 1, 1983, over the Soviet island of Sakhalin. All 269 passengers and crew were killed.
The plane had widely deviated from its course between Anchorage and northern Japan and flew over sensitive Soviet military installations in Kamchatka and Sakhalin.

The plaintiffs, who had been demanding a total of 510 million yen ($4.43 million) from the airline company, said they plan to appeal the ruling. They said U.S. courts had adopted tougher rulings against the airline company in the same case.
Families of the other 23 Japanese passengers killed in the incident have accepted out-of-court settlements or compensation from the airline company.
KAL's Japan branch spokesman said he will consult with the head office to decide whether or not to appeal the ruling.
"We renew our heartfelt condolences to the many victims who died in the incident," the spokesman said in a statement.
